We demonstrate that imposing a bounded exponent on a group significantly influences its structure. Specifically, we prove that if $G$ is a group with exponent $n$ possessing a $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup $A$, then there exists a genuine subgroup $H$ such that $H$ is finitely generated, commensurable with $H^k$, and $H$ closely approximates $A$ (i.e., $H \subset A \subset H^C$ for some constant $C$ depending on $k,r,n$). This finding extends the work of Breuillard, Gurevič, and Pyber, originally established for free groups. Furthermore, we establish that the size of such an approximate subgroup $A$ is limited by a polynomial determined by $k,r,n$, and $|A|/|H|$ is bounded by a rational function of these parameters and $n$.

This paper introduces novel algorithms based on randomized and Nesterov smoothing techniques for computing log-concave maximum likelihood estimators. These methods are shown to be asymptotically faster than the existing quasi-Newton approach, which is a significant advancement given the computational intensity of estimating log-concave distributions. Furthermore, we establish theoretical results demonstrating that the randomization-based algorithm converges to the maximum likelihood estimator at a rate of $O(n^{-1/3})$ in mean-squared error.

The non-interacting rigid model (NI-RAM), which assumes that force chains do not interact, has been utilized to predict the stability of granular assemblies. This study extends the model by incorporating the effects of anisotropy and finite grain size. We demonstrate that the model accurately forecasts the stability of granular materials, including those subjected to external magnetic fields, by accounting for the magnetic properties of the grains.

This paper examines a two-player game played on a directed graph, where vertices are colored either black or white. In each turn, the active player moves from their current vertex to an adjacent one. The game begins with the active player at a designated start vertex, $s$. The objective is to determine the minimum number of steps required to reach a target vertex, $t$, assuming both players play optimally. We refer to this minimum number as the game distance between $s$ and $t$. The game distance between two vertices that cannot reach each other via optimal play is defined as infinity. The set of all reachable game distances is termed the game distances of the graph. The primary focus of this work is to identify which non-negative integers and infinity can appear as game distances. The game is known in the literature as "black and white distance games" and was introduced by Cohen and colleagues in 2014.

The spectral density of stochastic processes is employed to differentiate between various random motions, such as Brownian motion and Lévy flights. Our study demonstrates that the spectral density of one-dimensional Lévy flights, characterized by an index $\alpha$ within the range $0 < \alpha < 1$, can be expressed as a definite integral. We also present a numerical method for calculating this density and compare our results with those reported in the literature.

This study examines the initial value problem for the integrable, soliton equation known as the higher-order Broer-Kaup (HOBK) system. The analysis relies on the integrable operator method, which establishes the solvability of this specific HOBK variant. The resulting operator is applied to construct a solution for the system. The research concludes by demonstrating the convergence of the derived integrable operator.

This paper investigates the conservation of energy in nonhomogeneous flows characterized by a gradient in density, focusing on the interaction between barotropic forces and buoyancy. We demonstrate that when these two forces are not aligned, energy is not conserved; however, if they act along the same line, a specific energy exchange occurs. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous proof of the well-posedness for the nonhomogeneous Navier-Stokes equations, valid for initial conditions in the critical Besov space.

This paper introduces VIRUP, a software package designed for simulating visual perception in virtual environments. Built on the premise that the creation of virtual settings is a core component of perceptual modeling, VIRUP offers a broad spectrum of tools for constructing such scenes. It enables users to define specific camera viewpoints and automate view sequences through Python scripting. Furthermore, the software facilitates the integration of visual data from various sources, including 3D models, physical renderings, and photographs. By providing a flexible and extensible architecture, VIRUP is designed to support the development of new features.

The Data Bricks Space Mission offers a free, hands-on learning experience designed to introduce children aged 8 to 12 to the fundamentals of data. This program, developed by the Data Bricks Foundation, empowers young learners to investigate planetary data, analyze it, and create their own visualizations. It is crafted to be an engaging introduction to data literacy and computational thinking, while simultaneously highlighting the critical role of data in scientific breakthroughs.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) offers a flexible framework for managing network traffic, yet it is susceptible to implementation errors and malicious attacks. Consequently, it is vital to verify that the traffic paths executed by an SDN controller align with the original specifications. This paper introduces a methodology for automatically generating test cases to validate SDN controllers. Our approach begins by analyzing the network topology and the controller's policy to construct a control-flow graph. We then apply graph-based search algorithms to this model to derive test cases that the controller should correctly process. Finally, we assess the proposed method through a case study involving a topology of 20 nodes and a single routing policy. Our results demonstrate that the generated test cases successfully traverse the control flow graph, covering every edge.

Generative models are frequently employed to create novel content by manipulating latent representations. However, the semantic meaning of these codes remains opaque, hindering precise and safe alterations. This study demonstrates that facilitating specific code changes relies on weak disentanglement, which partitions the latent space into interpretable subspaces. By applying this framework to StyleGAN2, we segmented the code into modules representing shape, texture, and color. This approach enables targeted editing of a single attribute while leaving others unaffected. Furthermore, the proposed method allows for the safe generation of novel images by restricting alterations to the neighborhood of a given latent code, thereby preventing unintended drift in other features.

This study utilizes large-eddy simulations to examine the flow dynamics around two oscillating flat plates, a configuration relevant to fish swimming and bird flight. The analysis focuses on the influence of varying phase differences on the flow field and the performance of the trailing foil. Results indicate that the strength of the leading edge vortices (LEVs) on the trailing foil is primarily dictated by the phase difference, whereas LEV interactions between the two foils mainly depend on the stroke amplitude. The performance of the trailing foil is significantly affected by the phase difference, which alters the LEV's position and its interaction with the trailing foil's trailing edge. Specifically, LEV interactions enhance thrust generation, whereas LEV–foil interactions diminish power consumption. Consequently, the propulsion efficiency peaks when the phase difference is 180° and the stroke amplitude is 30°.

Determining the real-axis spectral function from Euclidean time data is a fundamental challenge in real-time physics, yet current methods often fail due to the problem's ill-posed nature. We introduce a novel approach that utilizes a neural network to learn the inverse relationship between the spectral function and its Fourier transform on the imaginary axis, thereby enabling a robust reconstruction of the spectral function. This technique is demonstrated to be effective in extracting finite-temperature gluon propagators within Yang-Mills theory.

We propose that a quantum dot can serve as a sensor to map the addition spectrum of a superconductor. By utilizing a double-level system within the dot, we can selectively tune the system to probe specific energy states of the superconductor. When probing a single excited state, the resulting conductance reveals the superconducting gap, whereas measurements of a ground state allow for the determination of the superconducting quasiparticle density of states (QPDoS). We demonstrate that this approach is effective for characterizing the full addition spectrum of the superconductor. Furthermore, we illustrate that this methodology can be extended to characterize the quasiparticle density of states in topological superconductors.

The growing demand for pharmaceuticals has driven the development of computational methods to design drug molecules. While generative approaches have proven effective in creating molecules with desired properties, they often struggle to maintain structural constraints, such as specific substructures or isosteres. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that integrates a graph neural network with a reinforcement learning policy. This approach enables the generation of molecules that strictly adhere to predefined rules regarding molecular structure and target properties. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through ablation studies and practical applications, including the generation of analogs for existing drugs and the discovery of novel candidates targeting a specific protein.

This paper presents the Dynamic GoI Machine (DGoIM), a higher-order abstract machine designed to extend the GoI Machine (GoIM) \cite{GoIM} with dynamic capabilities. We situate DGoIM within Accattalli's classification of abstract machines \cite{Accattalli}, demonstrating that DGoIM is a variation of the GoIM, which itself is a variant of the BGM. By applying the operational correspondence between DGoIM and $\lambda_{dyn}$, we establish the consistency of DGoIM with $\lambda_{dyn}$, while also establishing the equivalence between the BGM and DGoIM. Furthermore, we establish the confluence of DGoIM and the completeness of the translation from $\lambda_{dyn}$ to DGoIM. Finally, we demonstrate that DGoIM is complete with respect to the completeness of the translation from $\lambda_{dyn}$ to DGoIM.

This study introduces a machine learning methodology for analyzing stellar populations in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) by leveraging the capabilities of the Gaia mission. We developed a novel algorithm that utilizes photometric data from both Gaia and the 2MASS catalog to classify stars into their respective evolutionary stages, including main-sequence, subgiant, and giant phases. This approach was applied to a sample of 1.5 million LMC stars, with the resulting classifications cross-referenced against the LMC stellar catalogue (LMCSC). The analysis reveals that the LMCSC's distance estimates for giants are biased by approximately 100 parsecs, whereas estimates for main-sequence stars are accurate to within 50 parsecs. Furthermore, we identified a new population of stars located in the LMC's halo, which exhibits a distinct spatial distribution compared to other LMC components. These findings demonstrate that machine learning can effectively enhance the study of stellar populations in the LMC.

This study introduces a novel approach to identifying electricity theft by leveraging the time-series characteristics of consumption data. We developed a deep learning framework that utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the interconnections between nodes within smart meter networks. By employing attention mechanisms, the system evaluates the significance of these connections to refine node representations, ultimately enhancing the detection of anomalous consumption patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in detecting electricity theft.

This paper extends the concept of sparse and tight surface graphs to tori. We establish a surface-graph analogue of the combinatorial Plücker formulas, utilizing it to analyze the incidence relations among algebraic varieties associated with toric arrangements. By leveraging the algebraic properties of the torus, we identify exactly 24 irreducible base graphs, proving that every sparse and tight graph on a torus can be constructed from these base graphs through a sequence of elementary operations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the number of irreducible base graphs is significantly fewer than the count of minimal generators found in the analogous problem for the planar case.

Using proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$, the $\Omega_c^0$ baryon was reconstructed via its decay into $\Xi_c^0 \pi^-$, with the $\Xi_c^0$ subsequently decaying into $K^+ \pi^- \pi^-$. The measured lifetime of the $\Omega_c^0$ is $27.3 \pm 1.3$ fs, which aligns with previous measurements but exhibits reduced uncertainty. The branching fraction ratio $\mathcal{B}(\Omega_c^0 \to \Xi_c^0 \pi^-)/\mathcal{B}(\Omega_c^0 \to \Xi_c^0 \pi^-)$ is determined to be $0.016 \pm 0.004$ (stat) $\pm$ 0.003 (syst).

Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC) is a prevalent unsupervised technique for partitioning data into distinct groups. Although existing SSC methods are effective, they suffer from high computational costs and fail to leverage spatial information, as they typically rely on the self-expressive property of data within a single subspace. To address these limitations, we introduce a new algorithm that simultaneously optimizes for self-expressiveness across multiple subspaces. This approach is achieved through a nonconvex optimization framework that employs a differentiable approximation for the $\ell_0$-norm. The proposed method is both computationally efficient and capable of handling large-scale datasets. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art SSC algorithms in clustering accuracy and execution speed.

This study introduces a new model for the thermal energy balance of sea ice incorporating melt ponds, which are essential for accurately simulating ice properties and the overall energy budget. The model integrates a novel parameterization for the ice albedo effect alongside a parameterization for the emissivity of the ice surface. By employing a one-dimensional heat conduction equation, the study calculates the temperature profile within the ice. The results demonstrate that including the effects of melt ponds significantly alters the energy balance, with the most pronounced impacts occurring during summer months.

We demonstrate that the shift in final spin projection during atom-molecule scattering can be mitigated by utilizing a Feshbach resonance to modulate the long-range potential. This approach is applicable to both single and dual atom-molecule systems. We also examine how these control mechanisms influence the generation of spin-polarized cold atoms.

This study demonstrates the link between the probability density function (PDF) governing the time evolution of the displacement in correlated anomalous diffusion and $q$-Gaussian distributions. Specifically, it establishes that $q$-Gaussians characterize the spatial distribution of displacements in systems exhibiting correlated anomalous diffusion. Furthermore, the work elucidates the specific conditions required for an evolving PDF to remain self-similar.

We present a novel proposal for a higher-order nodal line semimetal featuring robust surface Fermi arcs. In this system, the characteristics of the bulk nodal nodes and their corresponding surface Fermi arcs can be independently tuned. The study examines the magnetotransport behavior of this material, revealing a transition from conventional magnetoresistance to a quantum linear magnetoresistance (LMRM). This specific quantum LLMR emerges when the magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the nodal plane. The article concludes by discussing the potential practical applications of these findings.

This paper introduces a reputation management protocol designed for the Decentralized Computing System (DCCS), which is built upon the Decentralized Cloud (DDCC) platform. The DCCS is a distributed, peer-to-peer framework that ensures the reliability of decentralized systems by evaluating the trustworthiness of nodes. A core element of this protocol is the reputation score, which aggregates performance metrics from individual transactions to determine each node's trustworthiness. These scores are calculated by a dedicated algorithm that assesses node behavior during the execution of specific tasks. The DCCS leverages these scores to select the most reliable nodes for executing tasks, thereby enhancing the overall system's dependability.

This study introduces a linear perceptual quality assessment model for point clouds, designed to estimate visual quality through a linear combination of features derived from the 2D projections of the data. We evaluated this proposed model against various subjective quality scores and compared its efficacy with existing objective metrics. Experimental results indicate that the introduced method achieves a correlation coefficient of 0.81 with subjective ratings, outperforming current state-of-the-art solutions.

We investigate the Hawking-Page phase transition within the context of the gauge/gravity correspondence. By examining the thermodynamics of a five-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell theory featuring a scalar field, we demonstrate that the bulk phase transition corresponds to a first-order transition in the boundary's QCD-like model. Specifically, interpreting the black hole phase transition within the bulk aligns with the quarkyonic transition occurring in the dual theory.

This study introduces a novel, self-supervised deep learning framework designed to classify knee MRI scans for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and medial meniscus tears. The approach utilizes slice-based contrastive learning to pre-train a convolutional neural network, extracting slice-specific features that are subsequently fine-tuned on a small, labeled dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves an average accuracy of 88.5% in a two-class classification task (tear vs. non-tear). Furthermore, the framework exhibits robust performance across different MRI acquisition protocols, with an average accuracy of 84.5% when evaluated on data from three distinct sites. These findings suggest that the approach is highly effective for classifying knee MRI scans and adaptable to various imaging settings.

This study introduces a new font generation method that creates styled characters while preserving original content glyphs. Our approach employs a cross-attention mechanism to integrate the style into the structural elements of a content glyph. We demonstrate that the method effectively generates styled versions of content glyphs while maintaining their semantic meaning. Additionally, the system produces a coherent collection of characters that accurately reflect the intended style.

This study examines the covariant conservation of energy-momentum within a torsion-filled spacetime involving a charged fluid. The analysis incorporates the influence of torsion on the tensor structure, alongside the back-reaction effects of the electromagnetic field. Additionally, we derive the gravitational field equations for this charged fluid system.

This study introduces a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to optimize video streaming quality of experience (QoE) by intelligently selecting streaming parameters. The proposed DRL agent dynamically adjusts key variables—including bitrate, resolution, and frame rate—based on real-time network conditions and user-specific factors. By leveraging Q-learning, the agent learns an optimal policy that maximizes QoE while simultaneously minimizing buffer underflow and overflow incidents. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields superior QoE compared to existing methods, effectively balancing performance gains with the avoidance of buffering anomalies.

Neutrino astronomy is a rapidly advancing field, and the identification of $\nu_\tau$ remains a particularly significant and difficult objective. The $\tau$-appearance method, which utilizes the $\tau$-decay channel $K_L0 \to \mu^+\mu^-\pi^-$, is a leading candidate for discovering atmospheric $\tau$ neutrinos. This paper details a Monte Carlo simulation of the Super-Kamiokande detector, specifically tailored for the $\pi^-\pi^-$ channel, which is a critical component of the $\tau$-decay reconstruction. The simulation incorporates detector resolution and efficiency models derived from Super-Kamiokande data and applies a specific event selection strategy. Additionally, the study presents the results of a background estimation for the reconstructed $\pi^+\pi^-$ sample.

This paper investigates the quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a complex-valued potential, demonstrating well-posedness in $L^1_\mathbb{C}tL^2_x$ spaces. By employing the method of gauge transformation alongside the $L^2_t L^2_x$ Morawetz inequality, we establish global well-posedness for initial data with a bounded $L^1$-norm.

This paper investigates packet-level coding and scheduling across a multi-link network designed to efficiently transmit data flows generated periodically. The proposed scheduling algorithm utilizes link-specific Markovian models to forecast packet arrival times. Leveraging these predictions, the system employs packet-level coding to enhance transmission efficiency. Additionally, the system outlines a method for adaptively refining the Markovian model parameters based on observed incoming packets. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional scheduling approaches, particularly in scenarios characterized by predictable data sources.

The supernova explosion of Sgr A East occurred approximately 10,000 years ago at a distance of roughly 8 kiloparsecs from the Galactic center. This event created a supernova remnant (SNR) that is now expanding and interacting with the surrounding interstellar medium. The resulting interaction is expected to generate a hot, magnetized plasma, which is likely to emit synchrotron radiation. Observations of the region surrounding Sgr A East reveal a diffuse, extended radio source, designated as the "Sgr A East cocoon," which is a candidate for this emission. This paper presents a new analysis of the cocoon's radio spectrum, utilizing data from the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA). The spectral index derived from the VLA data is consistent with synchrotron emission, whereas the VLBA data indicates a flatter spectrum, suggesting that the VLBA observations are dominated by synchrotron self-absorption. This finding supports the conclusion that the VLBA emission originates from a compact source within the cocoon, likely a compact radio jet.

This study examines the impact of pre-trained language models on relation classification, specifically comparing two strategies: fine-tuning Transformer-based models from scratch versus training a classifier on top of frozen pre-trained model representations. While recent research indicates that fine-tuning generally yields superior results, we posit that the optimal approach is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the data and model. To evaluate this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis across various architectures and datasets, including both extensive and limited corpora. Our findings demonstrate that fine-tuning offers greater advantages on large datasets, whereas the second method proves more effective on smaller ones. Furthermore, we identified that the size of the pre-trained model is a critical factor, as larger models tend to produce better outcomes when fine-tuned.

The BEAT architecture is designed to enable Mobile Service Providers (MSPs) to share the expenses of infrastructure upgrades by leveraging a "pay-as-you-go" model. This approach allows MSPs to access and utilize additional resources from partner MSPs on demand, without needing to fund the expansion upfront. This paper investigates the stability of the BEAT architecture by modeling it as a game where each provider seeks to maximize its own utility. We demonstrate that for any number of providers, a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium exists. Furthermore, we prove that this game is a potential function game, which guarantees the existence of a pure-strategy equilibrium. Additionally, we analyze the impact of infrastructure investment costs on the equilibrium and the potential for multiple equilibria. Finally, we examine the influence of the pricing mechanism on the existence of multiple equilibria and conclude with an analysis of the BEAT architecture's scalability.

This study examines the spatial and temporal variations in the vorticity field within a two-dimensional, incompressible, turbulent flow. We introduce a novel approach to analyzing the Okubo-Weiss criterion by applying the Beltrami condition to the vorticity field, which allows us to link the criterion's components to the field's higher-order derivatives. This methodology enables the assessment of the criterion's evolution across both space and time.

This study examines the thermal characteristics of a Lee-Witt model featuring a singlet scalar and its associated right-handed neutrino. We analyze thermodynamic variables such as pressure, energy density, and the speed of sound within a two-phase framework: one dominated by Standard Model particles and the other by the Lee-Witt sector. While Standard Model particles interact with the Lee-Witt scalar, the Lee-Witt sector particles couple only to each other. We investigate the impact of these differing degrees of interaction on phase transitions, specifically addressing how the speed of sound influences the nature of the transition. Our findings indicate that the presence of the Lee-Witt scalar can trigger a crossover phase transition, whereas its absence results in a first-order transition.

Visual transformers have demonstrated remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, yet their standard self-attention mechanisms are computationally expensive and memory-intensive. While numerous optimization strategies have been introduced to mitigate these costs, they often fail to address the fundamental issue of processing excessive information. This paper introduces a novel methodology, StyTr$^2$, which leverages the power of style transfer to create a more efficient visual transformer. Unlike conventional approaches that handle all input data indiscriminately, StyTr$^2$ selectively processes only the most relevant features. This is achieved by applying style transfer to feature maps, thereby encoding semantic information into the style domain. Subsequently, a new attention mechanism is employed to identify and focus on the most pertinent features. Experimental results indicate that this approach not only significantly reduces computational overhead but also achieves superior accuracy compared to existing visual transformers.

We examine the design of optimal finite-time protocols for general thermodynamic systems, utilizing tools from thermodynamic geometry. The optimization focuses on two competing factors: the quantity of work extracted and the speed of the process. We demonstrate that this class of optimality conditions validates Heilmann's principle of thermodynamic geometry, which asserts that minimizing geometric distance between the initial and final states yields optimal paths. Furthermore, we establish that these findings hold across both equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems, encompassing a broad spectrum of models.

This study examines the discovery potential for a vector-like top partner ($T$) at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and the International Linear Collider (ILC) by analyzing the decay channel $T\bar{T} \to t\bar{t}b\bar{b}$. The analysis incorporates beamstrahlung effects and initial state radiation, alongside the use of the $t$-channel production mechanism. A key focus is the impact of the $T\bar{T}$ mass on the discovery reach. Furthermore, we investigate how varying the branching ratios of the $T\bar{T}$ decays influences the discovery potential. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the discovery potential across different collider scenarios.

This study investigates the dynamics of fluid redistribution in an acoustofluidic device driven by a traveling acoustic wave. The governing equations are derived from the Navier-Stokes framework, incorporating a time-dependent traveling wave as a body force. The analysis focuses on the specific case of a 2D channel with a small aspect ratio, where the flow is dominated by Stokes motion. Theoretical predictions regarding the critical acoustic energy density required for fluid relocation are validated through experimental data. The findings indicate that this threshold is inversely proportional to the square of the channel height and directly proportional to the square of the wavenumber. Additionally, the necessary density is shown to depend on the ratio of the Rayleigh number to the square of the Reynolds number.

This paper extends the classical Langer--Müller theorem, originally established for weighted shifts on directed semi-trees, to generalized directed semi-trees. The primary result demonstrates that every multiplication operator on a Hilbert space can be decomposed into a direct sum of weighted shifts defined on such generalized directed semi-trees. Utilizing this finding, we derive a novel Langer–Schröder theorem applicable to non-self-adjoint operators within a Hilbert space.

This study investigates the characteristics of positron pairs generated when ultra-short laser pulses strike high-Z targets. We examine how varying pulse durations and the longitudinal gradient of the laser field influence the energy spectra and angular distribution of the resulting positron ensembles. Our findings indicate that the energy spectra are highly sensitive to pulse duration, with the maximum energy of the positons increasing as the pulse shortens. Additionally, we analyzed the role of the longitudinal field gradient, noting that stronger gradients generally reduce the maximum energy of the positons. Notably, we observed that the angular distribution of the positons is heavily influenced by the specific pulse duration employed.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have proven highly effective for event prediction by leveraging graph structures to capture dependencies among event elements. However, existing graph-based methods often fail to adequately model the varying relevance of these connections, which can degrade performance. To address this, we introduce a Gating Mechanism Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GMCNN) that integrates a gating module to regulate information flow during GCNN operations. This gating mechanism dynamically adjusts the magnitude of information flow across the graph, thereby filtering out non-informative data and enhancing the model's ability to focus on pertinent information. Additionally, we implement a dual-channel feature extraction strategy to capture both local and global graph patterns. Experimental results on three public datasets demonstrate that GMCNN significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art graph-based approaches in event prediction tasks.

This study examines the impact of additive Gaussian noise applied to both features and responses in Bayesian linear regression. The analysis focuses on the widely used Gaussian process regression (GPR) model, which relies on a Gaussian likelihood and a Gaussian prior over the weights. The authors demonstrate that this scenario is mathematically equivalent to a standard GPR model with a specific variance-mixture prior, which can be expressed as a Laplace prior. Consequently, the posterior distribution for the weights in these scenarios is identical. The study further establishes that the predictive mean and variance for both formulations are equivalent, with the variance-mixture prior yielding a predictive mean that matches the GPR result under Laplace approximation. The analysis also explores the asymptotic behavior of the predictive variance, showing that it converges to zero as the number of features increases. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for Laplace regression and Gaussian process regression.

This study examines the impact of uncertainty on the physical parameters of quantum many-body systems, focusing on the realization of entangled states. We demonstrate that even minor inaccuracies in parameters can drastically reduce entanglement, causing the system to deviate from the optimal state. To address this, we introduce a feedback control scheme that dynamically adjusts these parameters to maximize entanglement. Our approach is validated through numerical simulations of the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) and the Transverse Field Heisenberg Model (TFHM).

This study introduces a technique for estimating the Jacobian of nonlinear systems using noisy spectral data derived from linearized operator samples. The approach builds upon the shift-invert Arnoldi method, which accelerates spectral estimation by leveraging shifts to enhance convergence rates. Theoretically, the paper demonstrates that the proposed method achieves an optimal convergence rate of $O(N^{-1})$ in $L^2$ norm, where $N$ denotes the sample count. Additionally, it is shown that the rate degrades to $O(N^{-1/2})$ when noise is present. The methodology is applied to estimate Jacobians within a deep neural network framework, offering a novel approach to weight estimation. The study further includes numerical experiments that evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness in scenarios involving both noise and limited data availability.

This work demonstrates that absorption coefficients within a one-dimensional semilinear transport equation can be recovered from absorption data derived from a single solution. The approach involves establishing a specific Lipschitz continuity property of this solution relative to the solution itself.

This article presents a comprehensive survey of explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) literature, offering a structured overview of key methodologies and applications. To facilitate deeper insight, we propose a new taxonomy for organizing existing XRL research. Our analysis reveals that current work primarily concentrates on post-hoc explanations, while identifying significant gaps in model transparency within reinforcement learning agents. Furthermore, we establish a new framework for future inquiry, emphasizing the necessity of aligning explanatory approaches with specific RL contexts and outlining practical steps for developing explainable agents.

We develop an axiom system for first-order lattice-valued logics by utilizing a functional representation theorem adapted from the methodology of Font, Jansana, and i Mend\'ez. This adaptation relies on the fact that every lattice-valued structure admits representation as an ultraproduct of lattice-valued Kripke frames. The resulting framework is defined by two key components: first, a specific set of first-order sequent calculus rules that are sound and complete relative to the semantic semantics of the frame-valued Kripke frames; and second, a mechanism for generating new axioms from existing ones through the application of first-order uniform substitutions.

This study examines the performance of a time-of-arrival (ToA)-based localization system in millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks, specifically focusing on the impact of node placement strategies. The research evaluates three distinct node deployment models: (i) nodes randomly scattered across the entire area, (ii) nodes randomly placed only within a specific sub-region, and (iii) nodes randomly distributed within a sub-region that is centrally located. The analysis reveals that the central placement strategy yields the most accurate localization results, followed by the sub-region approach, with random placement across the whole domain being the least effective. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the central strategy minimizes the mean localization error, and it establishes a direct link between this error and the variance of node locations.

Our analysis focuses on the regime where the interaction potential is not necessarily a short-range potential, but rather a potential that is bounded in $L^1$ and satisfies a specific bound on the $L^\infty$ norm of its Fourier transform. Under these premises, we prove that the dynamics of the system can be approximated by the dynamics governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii-Popov (GPP) equation. This study introduces a new approach to image completion that leverages the interplay between low- and high-frequency components. While existing methods typically address these components in isolation, our method restores texture fragments by integrating them with complementary fragments. To achieve this, we develop a novel frequency-adaptive network that utilizes a frequency-aware patch shuffling strategy to mix patches from different regions, thereby facilitating the joint reconstruction of low- and high-freq details. Additionally, we implement a multi-scale discriminator to enhance the realism of inpainted areas. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, with ablation studies confirming the efficacy of the proposed modules.

This study addresses the Thresholding Bandit problem, where the goal is to estimate an unknown threshold $\theta^*$ by minimizing the error probability, defined as the likelihood that the last selected arm $a_T$ satisfies $p_a > \theta^*$ but fails to meet the condition $p_{a_T} > \theta^*$. We establish an upper bound on the $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ probability of error and derive a lower bound on the $\Omega(\log T)$ tail of any algorithm's expected cost, where cost represents the count of arms with $p_a > \theta^*$ that are queried. We further demonstrate that the Bayes-optimal strategy achieves an $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ probability of error and an expected cost of $\Omega(\log T)$, with both metrics depending logarithmically on the number of arms $N$.

This work establishes a stability theorem for strictly mean convex hypersurfaces within the Riemannian setting, extending the findings of the 2D case presented in [1]. By adapting the method from [2], the authors establish robust stability results for these hypersurfaces in higher dimensions, thereby generalizing the established 2D conclusion found in [1].

This study examines the vortex-vortex distribution function in a two-dimensional superconductor with a square lattice structure. The analysis covers both the superfluid and normal phases, revealing a behavior that is independent of temperature: the vortices exhibit Gaussian distribution for separation distances smaller than the mean vortex separation, whereas they follow a power-law distribution at larger separations. The crossover between these regimes occurs at a power-law exponent of approximately 2.5, which aligns with the exponential decay of the superfluid order parameter's correlation length in the normal phase.

Public sentiment regarding artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving, significantly influencing the uptake of new technologies and the regulations that govern them. This paper introduces a novel framework for forecasting how the public will perceive emerging AI technologies. By leveraging a large language model, we analyze the text of news articles to derive features that represent each piece of coverage. We subsequently employ a machine learning model to forecast the predicted public opinion score based on these textual features. Our proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 75% on the test set, outperforming baseline methods. Furthermore, we examine the specific characteristics of the extracted news features and their impact on the prediction outcomes.

This study reports the first observation of the $\Xi_c^0 \rightarrow \pi^- \Lambda_c^+$ decay mode, utilizing data from $pp$ collisions collected by the LHCb detector at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 1 $\text{fb}^{-1}$. The branching fraction for this decay is determined to be $(4.40 \pm 0.52) \times 10^{-3}$, relative to the $\Xi_c^0 \rightarrow \Lambda(\pi^- \pi^-)$ channel.

This study introduces an approximation technique designed to address hybrid nonlinear equations. The work includes the formulation of an iterative algorithm and the proof of its convergence under specific conditions. Additionally, numerical examples are provided to validate the theoretical findings.

Safety is paramount in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly when agents operate within complex, real-world environments. However, standard RL algorithms often struggle to adhere to safety requirements, leading to frequent constraint breaches. To address this, we introduce a novel method that integrates a learned safety policy with the agent's primary policy. This secondary policy is trained to minimize the agent's reward function, thereby reducing the likelihood of violating safety constraints. Our approach utilizes a new loss function that penalizes actions likely to result in violations, encouraging the agent to avoid such behaviors. Additionally, we incorporate a dynamic noise injection mechanism that adapts the noise level based on the agent's proximity to a safety violation. This mechanism helps the agent explore safer regions of the state-action space and mitigates the risk of overfitting to specific constraints. Empirical results on various safety-sensitive RL tasks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines in terms of both safety and performance.

This study investigates the superradiant phase transition in chiral light within a system of two-level atoms driven by a single-mode coherent field. We demonstrate that under conditions of strong driving, a distinct chiral superradiant phase emerges, characterized by a non-zero photon current circulating around the atomic ring. This phase can be described as a spontaneous breaking of combined parity and time-reversal symmetry. Furthermore, we show that increasing the driving strength lowers the critical coupling required for the superradiant transition. Additionally, the phase diagram reveals an intricate interplay between the chiral superradiant phase and the standard first-order superradiant transition. Finally, the phase diagram is shown to be tunable by adjusting the coherent field's phase.

This paper introduces a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework utilizing a Transformer to facilitate agent coordination. The approach employs a two-layer architecture: the lower layer utilizes Level-Adaptive QTransformers (LAQTransformers) to derive action policies based on varying agent levels, while the upper layer learns a centralized value function to predict long-term rewards. The proposed method, termed Transformer Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (TH-MARL), is evaluated on a multi-agent resource allocation task. Experimental results demonstrate that TH-MARL surpasses both flat QMIX and standard hierarchical variants. Notably, the method exhibits greater scalability with respect to the number of agents and demonstrates improved robustness against communication noise.

This study introduces a new framework for deep reinforcement learning (DRL) tailored to particle robot systems, addressing the computational hurdles that typically limit DRL scalability in large swarms. By leveraging a particle filter, we enable the learning process to operate on aggregated states rather than individual entities, effectively reducing the state space dimensionality. Consequently, this approach allows robots to collaborate effectively even when their numbers are orders of magnitude higher than feasible with existing DRL methods. We validate the viability of this framework through simulations of particles moving in unidirectionally to maximize coverage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework is robust to variations in particle scale and can be adapted for diverse tasks, such as coordinated formation control.

The exoplanet WASP-31b, characterized by its extreme temperature, serves as a critical test case for understanding the atmospheric physics of hot Jupiters. This study utilizes the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to conduct a comprehensive analysis of its atmosphere, specifically focusing on the 3.3 $\mu$m region. By employing a Bayesian framework, we examine the impact of clouds on observable spectral features, including water and atomic signatures. Our findings indicate that clouds are essential for reproducing the observed data; notably, they diminish the depth of the water absorption band and the strength of the atomic potassium feature. Furthermore, we observe a significant discrepancy between the abundances of potassium and water derived from the spectrum, which we attribute to cloud-induced effects.

HPC-as-a-Service (HPCaaS) has emerged as a promising avenue for delivering high-performance computing capabilities through cloud infrastructure. However, the HPC ecosystem has traditionally resisted the cloud due to the high computational demands of many applications. This study examines the performance characteristics of HPCaaS by analyzing the behavior of tightly coupled applications running on cloud-based HPC platforms. The research investigates two primary variables: the quantity of concurrent application instances and the level of contention among instances. Results indicate that HPCaaS is best suited for low-instance deployments when handling large-scale, tightly coupled workloads, as increased contention significantly degrades performance. Conversely, for loose coupling tasks, the platform can effectively handle multiple simultaneous instances with only moderate performance penalties. These findings offer critical guidance for optimizing application configurations within HPCaaS environments.

This study introduces a new approach to analyzing patient similarity by integrating the functional connectivity (FC) graphs of individual patients. The method begins by constructing a graph for each subject, where nodes represent brain regions and edges indicate functional links. These FC graphs are then transformed into graph signal processing (GSP) graphs, which are used to extract features for comparing pairs of patients. The resulting pairwise similarity scores are evaluated against clinical outcomes to determine their diagnostic utility.

To assess the approach's effectiveness, we conducted a comparative analysis of two distinct methods: one that incorporates the topological structure of FC graphs and another that relies solely on the edge weights. Our findings indicate that the proposed method, which includes topological information, outperforms the existing graph-based approach. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the method is sensitive to topological structure, as it can effectively differentiate heterogeneous patient pairs from homogeneous ones. Additionally, we examined the impact of various graph signal processing kernels on the approach's performance.

This paper presents a novel application of the Milgram Gauss sum formula to calculate signatures (modulo 8) for non-singular forms defined over $\mathbb{Z}$, particularly when the underlying matrix is sparse. The proposed method is broadly applicable to numerous graph structures, with a specific focus on trees and forests.

This study explores the feasibility of detecting X-ray Transition Radiation (XTR) using the newly developed, high-performance, high-gradient superconducting accelerating structure known as the "Superconducting Elliptical Resonator" (SER). The SER, which is currently under construction at the Advanced Test Stand (ATS) facility within Fermilab, is designed to produce intense electron beams with high energy density. The experiment's primary objective is to capture XTR generated by these electron beams as they transition from the SER into a vacuum pipe. The analysis involves a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates the specific electromagnetic field distributions within the SER with the established model of transition radiation. The results indicate that the experimental data align well with theoretical predictions, confirming the validity of this approach. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of various operational parameters on the XTR yield, including beam energy, beam current, and the specific dimensions of the SER.

The human capacity to comprehend language relies on the ability to infer the meaning of sentences. While this process is intuitive for humans, it remains a significant hurdle for computational systems. A primary challenge lies in the fact that a sentence's meaning is not entirely encapsulated within its explicit arguments; rather, it depends on context, allowing the listener to infer unmentioned roles. For instance, in "John saw Mary's car," the car itself is not described, yet its significance is clear. Similarly, in "John ate his breakfast early," the time of consumption is not stated but implied by the temporal adverb. Capturing these implicit details is essential for generating a full semantic understanding. This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying these unmentioned arguments, termed "implicit argument detection." We propose a new dataset for this purpose and develop a model capable of predicting these missing roles. Our results demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art benchmarks.

This study introduces a new framework for detecting tuberculosis in chest X-rays, which simultaneously localizes the lungs and classifies the disease. We propose a specialized loss function that encourages the localization confidence scores to increase as the probability of tuberculosis decreases. This approach yields more precise lung localization and reduces false positive regions. Furthermore, the proposed loss function integrates lung localization directly into the identification process, eliminating the need for separate pre-processing steps. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a F1-score of 0.942 on the public CheXpert dataset.

This article introduces penalized minimum Hellinger distance statistics designed for model selection in finite samples. The approach involves augmenting the data with an additional observation that encodes model-specific information, such as sign patterns of residuals, to capture model uncertainty. By integrating this augmented data into a minimum Hellinger distance framework, the method generates penalized tests for model selection, effectively balancing model fit and complexity. The resulting penalized minimum Hellinger distance criterion functions as a robust, adaptive model selection tool that balances model fit and parsimony. Simulations demonstrate the method's superior performance compared to conventional minimum Hellinger distance statistics in finite samples, with applications shown in selecting robust models for linear and generalized linear frameworks.

This paper investigates the recurrence characteristics of the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence, demonstrating that specific finite binary patterns manifest within the sequence through mechanisms distinct from the usual method of containment in its shifts. It further establishes that the count of such occurrences for a binary pattern of length $n$ grows asymptotically as $n^{5/2}$, and it provides an explicit characterization of all such patterns.

Cost-sensitive hierarchical clustering (CSHC) involves a scenario where a sequence of clustering algorithms is applied to a dataset, with each algorithm incurring a fixed cost upon execution. This problem is closely linked to algorithm selection, where specific models are chosen for particular datasets to minimize expenses. This work introduces a new algorithm for selecting cost-sensitive clustering algorithms, utilizing Bayesian machine learning to predict the optimal method for a given dataset. This algorithm employs a Gaussian process (GP) to model the relationship between feature characteristics and the rank of algorithms based on their clustering quality. Experiments on various real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in selecting appropriate cost-sensitive clustering algorithms.

The 21cm signal from neutral hydrogen during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR) is anticipated to be extremely faint, with an intensity roughly one millionth that of the Cosmic Microwave Background. Consequently, extracting this signal from the foreground contamination of bright radio sources remains a significant challenge. This study investigates the application of deep learning techniques to isolate the EoR signal from simulated data. We employed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on simulated 21cm maps to classify data into either EoR or foreground categories. The model was evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall. The results indicate that the CNN effectively distinguishes between the two classes, successfully identifying the EoR signal in various simulated scenarios.

This study presents a systematic investigation into the electronic and magnetic characteristics of monolayer and bilayer forms of $MX_2$ ($M = \text{Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba}$; $X = \text{F, Cl, Br}$) materials. Our findings indicate that all monolayer and bilayer configurations exhibit semiconducting behavior, with band gaps ranging from 1.0 to 3.0 eV. Notably, the bilayers of $MX_2$ demonstrate robust stability, whereas the monolayers are found to be unstable. Furthermore, we identified that $\text{CaF}_2$ bilayers and $\text{CaF}_2$ monolayers possess Curie temperatures ($T_c$) exceeding room temperature, with values of 210 K and 120 K, respectively. These results suggest that $\text{CaF}_2$ bilayers and monolayers are viable candidates for spintronic applications.

This study establishes the positive definiteness of functions defined on the product of quasi-metric spaces, thereby demonstrating that such Cartesian products functionally admit both an injective and non-isometric separable Hilbert space embedding.

The study of positive monoids has long been a vibrant area of research, with significant recent interest directed toward monoids generated by geometric sequences. This work establishes a sufficient and necessary condition for the submonoid $\langle \{1, x, y, y^2x, y^3x, y^4x, ...\} \rangle$ to be contained within the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$.

Case description data, often found in case-control studies, can enhance sensitivity toward potential hidden biases in examining exposure-disease relationships. This study evaluates a novel approach utilizing this data by applying it to a recent investigation into the link between childhood obesity and asthma. The analysis focuses on a sample of 1,000 children with asthma and 1,000 controls, utilizing a case description-based weighting method to estimate the association between obesity and asthma while allowing for an assessment of sensitivity toward hidden bias. The results demonstrate that incorporating case description data yields a more precise estimation of the odds ratio compared to traditional methods, while also providing clearer insights into how hidden bias might influence the study's conclusions.

We establish a proven conjecture regarding the equality of two functors: Chow groups of 0-cycles and Suslin homology, operating over finitely generated fields with a generic characteristic. This validation clarifies several aspects of the $K_0$- Chow theory for normal projective schemes.

This study presents measurements of the inclusive production cross-sections for $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV. The analysis focuses on the midrapidity region ($|y| < 0.9$) and includes the differential distributions with respect to transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) and rapidity ($y$). These results are compared to previous data from the LHCb experiment at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV. Additionally, the study examines the dependence of the mean transverse momentum on event multiplicity, revealing a rise in the mean $p_{\rm T}$ for both $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ states as particle multiplicity increases. The measured cross-sections are evaluated against theoretical predictions from the Color Glass Condensate and Color Glass Condensate models, as well as the Color Glass Condensate model. We introduce a novel measurement protocol for determining the entropy of spin-1/2 systems, which surpasses the capability of prior methods that were limited to analyzing a single component. By employing a technique that integrates measurements across varying bases, we successfully measure the entropy of any sub-system within a quantum state. This approach is validated through an experiment involving a quantum state distributed among three qubits, where we accurately calculate the entropies of both individual qubits and every possible pair.
This study presents a new approach to the Geometric Principle of Moduli, which has been utilized to demonstrate classical theorems from analytic theory using elementary analytic functions.

This study examines the discrete Schrödinger equation featuring both long-range interactions and a nonlinear term with soft or hard confinement. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, the equation admits a family of stationary solutions, or solitons, which are both stable and long-lived. By employing the variational method, we analyze the existence of these localized structures. Furthermore, we establish that when the soft nonlinearity is of the power type, the normed space of such solutions is compact. In scenarios where soft confinement is absent, we identify specific conditions ensuring the existence of solitary solutions that minimize the associated energy functional. Additionally, we prove that the set of such energy-minimizing solutions forms a compact set.

Signomial programming is a specific type of mathematical optimization that is non-convex, yet it can be effectively addressed using the Multivariate (MM) algorithm. This approach relies on the majorization-minimization (MM) principle, which alternates between replacing a difficult objective function with a simpler, lower-bound approximation and solving a resulting convex sub-problem. This process guarantees convergence to a stationary point. The MM algorithm is highly versatile, as it can be applied to various signomial programming formulations, including those with inequality constraints, by converting them into equivalent equality constraints first. This paper introduces a new MM-based method for signomial programming that directly handles inequality constraints. This method is derived from the signomial programming formulation with inequality constraints converted to equality constraints, which is then solved using the standard MM algorithm. Although hyperbolicity is a well-known concept in complex geometry, a hyperkähler manifold can never be Kobayashi hyperbolic due to its structure. This paper investigates a specific hyperkähler four-manifold by analyzing it through various lenses, including its hyperbolic features, to understand how these manifolds relate to hyperbolicity.

We introduce a new approach for generating personalized 3D avatars from scratch using only a single image and an arbitrary depth map. Our method employs a multi-stage framework that progressively refines the avatar's geometry and texture. To address the challenges posed by noisy and incomplete depth data, we utilize a multi-resolution representation that captures details at varying scales. This approach ensures that texture is accurately aligned with geometry across all resolutions, enabling the final avatar to exhibit high-fidelity surface details. Additionally, we develop a multi-stage refinement process that progressively sharpens the avatar's geometry. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both visual quality and geometric accuracy.

This study introduces a new face de-occlusion technique that utilizes a 3D morphable model (3DMM) to reconstruct occluded facial regions. By leveraging the 3DMM, our approach generates high-fidelity 3D representations of faces, which are subsequently projected onto the 2D image plane to fill missing areas. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios involving dense occlusions.

Intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising pathway for balancing learning and exploration, challenging the conventional reliance on random or model-based techniques. This study introduces a novel RL framework grounded in intrinsically motivated, self-supervised learning objectives. By utilizing a hierarchy of skills that encodes intrinsic rewards, the proposed agent achieves a more efficient balance between acquiring new behaviors and deploying existing capabilities. Empirical evaluations on the MuJoCo benchmark demonstrate that this approach surpasses both model-based and random exploration methods. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robustness to environmental stochasticity and supports flexible task adaptation.

This study examines a fully distributed, policy iteration algorithm designed for the centralized Markov decision process (MDP) in a networked environment. In this framework, each agent manages a specific subset of state variables and seeks to optimize its portion of the global objective. Agents operate in a fully distributed manner, utilizing only local communications with neighbors to execute the algorithm. We demonstrate that the optimality gap incurred by this approximate method diminishes as the size of each agent's local neighborhood expands. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound on this gap, showing it is proportional to the square of the total state space size divided by the square of the local neighborhood size.

This study examines the characteristics of events devoid of charged particles, a category that is notably absent in standard predictions derived from calculations assuming exclusive color-singlet exchange. However, when analyzed against data from the UA2 experiment, these events align closely with predictions generated by Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate hadronic final states.

The electronic band structure of penta-silicene is highly tunable through external electric fields, which renders it a highly promising candidate for optoelectronic applications. This tunability stems from the material's unusual band structure, which is distinct from that of conventional materials. To understand the underlying physics, we have analyzed the electronic band structure of penta-silicene using a tight-binding model. Our findings indicate that the penta-silicene lattice is composed of two interpenetrating triangular sublattices, which are responsible for its unique characteristics. Furthermore, we have identified the specific elements of the Hamiltonian matrix that are non-zero. These elements are crucial for describing the electronic properties of penta-silicene under the influence of an electric field.

This study examines the thermal dissociation of bottom quarkonium within a fractional-order thermal medium, utilizing the Schr\"odinger equation to model the bound state. We employ the Cornell potential, incorporating both the strong Coulombic and linear confining interactions, to describe quarkonium dynamics. The analysis reveals that increasing the fractional parameter elevates the decomposition temperature of heavy quarkonium states.

The standard cosmological model posits that dark matter is distributed in a clumpy fashion, with large-scale structures composed of subhalos. These subhalos, which are significantly more massive than individual atoms, may have collided with Earth in the distant past. Such impacts would have been far more violent than those from asteroids or comets, potentially leaving detectable physical traces in geologic materials. This study examines the feasibility of identifying these ancient dark matter collisions by analyzing the isotopic composition of terrestrial rocks. We demonstrate that, for subhalos exceeding 1000 Earth masses, the resulting spallation of atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen could generate a measurable excess of deuterium. Furthermore, we establish that the magnitude of this deuterium anomaly is inversely proportional to the square of the time elapsed since the event. Consequently, we anticipate that forthcoming high-precision measurements of deuterium abundances in ancient rocks could reveal evidence of dark matter interactions dating back to the early solar system.

This paper investigates coordinated patrolling within a networked environment, specifically addressing scenarios where the network topology is uncertain. We introduce a novel patrolling framework that integrates a communication layer with a decision-making layer. The topology module utilizes a Bayesian network to update beliefs regarding the network structure, whereas the decision-making module employs reinforcement learning to generate patrolling policies based on these beliefs. We evaluate this approach against a baseline strategy that ignores network uncertainty. The results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the baseline, particularly in environments characterized by high uncertainty.

This paper introduces a novel framework for robot navigation that integrates the strengths of both model-based and model-free approaches. It achieves this by utilizing a learned policy to derive action priors, which are then fused with an existing model-based planner. This hybridization enables the system to operate effectively in unstructured, real-world environments. Experimental evaluations across three distinct domains—simulated settings, real-world office spaces, and public street environments—demonstrate that our method significantly boosts navigation success rates and improves trajectory smoothness compared to prior art. Furthermore, the study provides a quantitative analysis of the trade-off between trajectory quality and learning efficiency, along with a discussion on the advantages of the proposed approach.

This study examines the magnetic phase diagram of a dipole ensemble situated on a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice. By employing a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and analytical methods, we delineate the system's phase diagram, which encompasses the ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and disordered states. Furthermore, we analyze the dynamic scaling of the correlation length and susceptibility near the critical points. Our results indicate that the dynamic critical exponents align with those observed in the three-dimensional Heisenberg model.

This study addresses the task of identifying a homogeneous inclusion with constant conductivity within a domain using exterior measurement data. It is established that such an inclusion can be uniquely determined up to coordinate transformations, provided the measurements are available for an arbitrary set of at least two distinct transmitters and receivers. Furthermore, the inclusion can be recovered if a single transmitter and a single receiver are allowed to move across the domain's exterior boundary, again given two distinct locations for each.

This study examines the dynamics of the higher-order Kuramoto model across simplicial frameworks. We demonstrate that these dynamics can be interpreted as gradient flows within a suitable metric space. Leveraging these findings, we introduce a novel algorithm for computing the minimal spanning tree of a simplicial complex, utilizing the properties of gradient flows.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamental operation in scientific computing, yet its performance remains highly sensitive to architectural and software-level factors. To optimize SpMV implementation across diverse hardware, one must determine the most effective memory layout, the ideal granularity for data partitioning, and the most suitable communication strategy. This paper presents a unified framework for SpMV that simultaneously addresses layout selection, data partitioning, and communication methods. By modeling the trade-offs between these variables, we derive an analytical expression for execution time. Leveraging this model, we developed a heuristic algorithm capable of identifying a near-optimal configuration for a specific problem on a given architecture. Experimental results on various sparse matrices and a range of HPC systems demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving performance gains of up to 2.5×.

This study establishes a shared point relationship between two families of meromorphic functions: one shares a general meromorphic function $g$ with $M$ distinct poles (with multiplicity at least $m$), while a second function shares a specific value $a$ as an $m$-value. We demonstrate that if such a normal family of meromorphic functions shares its general meromorphic function with at least $m$ distinct poles of sufficient multiplicity, and simultaneously shares the constant $a$ with multiplicity at least $m$, then it must be a normal family of meromorphic functions.

Intention recognition serves as a vital component of human-robot collaboration (HRC), yet its application in real-world settings is often hindered by overly complex robotic hardware. This study addresses the challenge of recognizing intentions within a simplified robot framework, specifically one equipped with a single fixed-mounted camera. We introduce a new approach that integrates the recognition of intentions with the planning of robot movements. This method employs a hierarchical architecture comprising two layers: a top-level module that predicts the user's intent and a bottom-level module that generates planning trajectories based on that prediction. By unifying these processes, the system enhances overall performance. Furthermore, we developed a specialized dataset to train and evaluate this approach. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior outcomes compared to conventional techniques that treat intention recognition and motion planning independently.

This study demonstrates that homogeneous Monge-Ampère systems represent a bridge between isothermal, barycentric, and projective geometries. We establish that within such systems, triples of conjugate points across these three contexts form Lagrangian pairs. Furthermore, our findings are applied to investigate the Laplace transform's geometric framework. We establish a connection between the classical conjugate points of isothermal and barycentric spaces and those appearing in the geometric definition of the Laplace transform. Additionally, our work reveals a dual relationship between the geometric formulations of the Laplace transform and the Abel-Jacobi map.

This study investigates the influence of solutally induced natural convection on the dissolution of gas bubbles in water using a novel experimental approach. By employing a custom-built apparatus, we successfully isolated the effect of convection on dissolving bubbles, demonstrating that neglecting this mechanism leads to a significant overestimation of the mass transfer coefficient. The research establishes a new correlation for mass transfer coefficients that incorporates the effects of natural convection, thereby enhancing the accuracy of mass transfer models used in gas-liquid systems.

This study presents a search for supersymmetry within the final states containing two jets, one lepton, and missing transverse momentum, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The dataset is analyzed under the framework of the gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking (GMSB) model, specifically targeting the decay of a neutralino into a gravitino and a $W$ boson. Signal regions are defined based on the invariant mass of jet-lepton pairs and the transverse momentum of the leading jet. Exclusion limits are established for various proper decay lengths, ranging from $10^{-12}$ to $10^4$ seconds. For decay times of $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-9}$ seconds, the neutralino mass upper limit is determined to be $370$ GeV, $400$ GeV, and $410$ GeV, respectively.
